incidents.title: Incident with Pull Requests

updates.body:
On November 16, 2026, between 09:30 and 15:55 UTC, some pull request merges on GitHub timed out. On average, 2.9% of merge attempts timed out, with a peak of 7.1% at 15:17 UTC. Some GitHub Actions workflow runs triggered by pull requests were also delayed. Git operations such as push and fetch stayed available, with higher latency. This was a repeat of a shorter event on November 13, between 13:15 and 17:50 UTC, when 1.7% of merges timed out.

Both events had the same cause: some of the storage servers that hold Git repository data reached their disk read bandwidth limits. A merge must be written to every copy of a repository, so one overloaded server slowed merges for every repository it hosts. Read load on these servers had been growing as part of a planned move of repositories to new infrastructure. A disk configuration setting on those servers also made them read far more data than necessary, which cut their usable bandwidth roughly in half. We mitigated the incident by correcting that setting and moving some load away from the busiest servers.

The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. We are adding storage capacity in the affected region and alerting on per-server disk bandwidth so we catch saturation before it affects customers. Sustained merge timeouts will now page our on-call engineers directly. We are also adding capacity checks before moving repositories or traffic onto new infrastructure.

incidents.title: Impact across multiple GitHub products including Actions, Pages, and Copilot products.

updates.body:
On November 11, 2026, from 20:05 to 21:02 UTC, customers experienced delayed or failed Actions workflow starts, webhook errors and delivery delays, slower GitHub Apps API requests, and reduced availability of Copilot features, including Code Review. GitHub Pages builds were also delayed.

Nearly all GitHub Actions runs triggered between 20:18 and 20:55 UTC were delayed or failed, leaving approximately 3.4 million partially created runs that are being canceled. No GitHub Pages deployments completed during the incident. In the Central US data residency stamp, between 20:06 and 20:50 UTC, about 63% of webhook API requests failed and 27% of deliveries were not recorded; those deliveries reached their destinations but remain unavailable to view or redeliver. Between approximately 20:20 and 21:00 UTC, Copilot code review on github.com completed 87% fewer reviews than normal and some other Copilot features were also unavailable.

The disruption was caused by an Azure Cosmos DB regional outage affecting database accounts used by these services. Per Cosmos’s RCA, a configuration change to the Central US gateways exposed a latent race condition under a specific high-load traffic pattern, causing gateway crashes and health-probe failures. Cosmos mitigated by rolling back the change. Service health recovered around 21:02 UTC, and the queued Actions backlog finished processing by 21:21 UTC.

Our follow-up work focuses on validating regional database failover across affected services and developing tested recovery procedures. We are also improving recovery tools to quickly clear stuck Actions checks and runs after incidents so they do not remain uncancelable or block pull request merges.

updates.body:

The temporary limits also restricted access to commit pages for users who were not signed in. Background processing continued to catch up after service health recovered.

We have reduced repeated repository-analysis work and are adding workload-level concurrency controls to better protect customer-facing requests. We are also improving our procedures for safely reducing background load and making pull request synchronization more resilient to temporary failures.

incidents.title: Incident with Actions and Checks API

updates.body:
On November 9, 2026, between 18:07 and 18:59 UTC, GitHub Actions experienced degraded performance. During this time, some customers saw workflow runs fail to start, update or report status correctly. An average of 28% of workflow runs were affected, peaking at 65% during the worst period of the incident. Once Actions services recovered, some jobs were left in a state that limited available concurrency until the runs were released.

The incident occurred during a planned migration of a core Actions database from GitHub’s datacenter to a new cloud region. After the migration completed, we shifted Actions service traffic to the new region. The volume of requests exceeded the capacity and rate limits configured there, so a portion of requests were rejected and workflow updates failed. Dependent services, including Webhooks, Pages and Copilot code review, saw secondary impact.

We mitigated impact by shifting some of the traffic back to the original region, allowing service traffic to remain within the configured limits. We then increased capacity and rate limits in the new region before gradually shifting traffic back. While this was a one-time migration event for this cluster that is now complete, we are improving how we validate capacity and limits before shifting traffic during remaining migrations, including shifting traffic in smaller steps. To address the stuck runs left after the incident, we are improving our ability to detect and mitigate these runs for future cases as well as readying an API to enable customers to address this themselves.

updates.body:

incidents.title: Incident with Git Operations, Pull Requests and Actions

updates.body:
On October 7, 2026, GitHub had two outages of write operations with the same cause, totaling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC (about 10 minutes) and the second from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC (about 9 minutes). In both windows, actions that save or change data failed across Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. Reading data was largely unaffected.

In the first outage, 5.6% of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9%, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26% of Git authentication requests failed, and 17% of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second outage, 6.2% of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3%, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25% of Git authentication requests failed, and 19% of Actions workflow runs failed. No databases experienced data loss, and operations retried after recovery succeeded.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records, which still listed database servers we had already retired. When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers.

Each outage ended when one of our established machines with correct configuration became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. After the first outage, we identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. At 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honor the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again. We shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and have since removed it, and the automation now honors the pause, which was a new regression due to an update of our puppet infrastructure.

To prevent recurrence, we are clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, and we are keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked. We are also changing our systems to reject configuration that point to servers that don't exist and to keep using the last known-good settings instead. Finally, we are giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

We will share a more detailed write-up of these incidents in our monthly availability report, along with the status of the repairs we are making to prevent issues like these in the future.

updates.body:
On November 16, 2026, between 09:30 and 15:55 UTC, some pull request merges on GitHub timed out. On average, 2.9% of merge attempts timed out, with a peak of 7.1% at 15:17 UTC. The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. On October 22, 2026, between 14:55 and 17:28 UTC, search on GitHub.com was degraded. Search-backed features in Issues, Pull Requests, Projects, Actions, Packages, and some REST API endpoints returned errors or incomplete results. On average, 21% of search requests failed, peaking at 52%. Running Actions workflows, uploading and downloading packages, and Git operations were not affected.

This was due to the proxies that route requests to our search clusters running out of CPU while setting up encrypted connections. Requests that timed out were retried, which added more load and kept the proxies overloaded. The search clusters themselves remained healthy.

We mitigated the incident by adding proxy capacity, after which search recovered at 17:28 UTC.

We have started reducing the CPU cost of these encrypted connections. We are also working to make search retries adjustable during an incident without a deployment, and to alert on search failures sooner. Together these will reduce our time to detection and mitigation of issues like this one in the future.

incidents.title: Incident with Actions

updates.body:
On October 22, 2026, from 13:05 to 15:20 UTC, our event streaming platform was degraded resulting in elevated job processing latency spikes of 19-35 seconds and elevated job processing times of 4m – this resulted in delayed Actions workflow and step results (up to 13m), notifications (20m) and repository push events (12m). Recovery for repositories began at 14:32, with Actions recovery beginning at 14:59. The issue reoccurred at 16:26 again impacting Actions runs, repo push events, and notifications. Recovery began at 17:16 and completed at 2:07.

The incident was caused by a significant increase in load coupled with client connection storms during a deployment overloading our Kafka event streaming brokers.

To prevent future recurrence, we have expanded the affected cluster, shifted traffic to less loaded clusters, and implemented tunable client reconnect backoff.

incidents.title: Delays for Pull Requests and Webhook deliveries

updates.body:
On October 21, 2026, between 13:22 UTC and 19:22 UTC, several GitHub services were delayed due to degradation of our internal event streaming platform.

Pull request updates, push webhooks, and push-triggered Actions workflows were delayed by up to 33 minutes until 15:36 UTC. Actions status updates were delayed by up to 33 minutes until 16:16 UTC, holding up some merges and deployments that wait on checks. Webhook deliveries and live updates were delayed by up to 25 minutes until 16:52 UTC. Audit log events were delayed by up to two hours.

This was due to servers in the platform running out of memory caused by client reconnections without sufficient retry backoff. We mitigated the incident by moving the busiest workloads to less-loaded servers and adding capacity.

We have since added reconnection backoff and added server capacity. We are building a solution for auto-rebalancing connections across servers, and splitting the platform into smaller, isolated clusters to reduce blast radius and time to mitigation of issues like this one in the future.

incidents.title: Degraded availability for GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages and Webhooks

updates.body:
On October 19, 2026, between 15:24 and 16:52 UTC, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, and webhooks generated by Actions were degraded. Live updates on GitHub.com and code search were also degraded for part of this time. No data was lost.

Impact

- Workflow status updates, logs, and checks were delayed.
- 5.13% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners were delayed in starting, and 0.02% of workflow runs failed.
- During the first 30 minutes, 8.47% of requests to the Actions jobs REST API returned errors.

Pages deployments and webhooks generated by Actions runs were delayed.

An internal Actions service that stores logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region and immediately retried them from every server at once. The resulting surge of new connections overloaded a shared network link between our data center and that region, which also disrupted other services that use the same link. We mitigated the incident by moving the Actions service off the affected cache servers and reducing connections from other services on the link. We then processed the delayed Actions work. We are continuing to investigate the cause of the initial connection timeouts.

We were already in the process of rolling out a limit on how quickly this service can open new connections, but it was still in shadow mode (logging only, not enforcing) at the time of the incident. We have since fully enforced it and capped the service's concurrent connection attempts. We are extending these limits to other Actions services, adding backoff to retries, limiting how much shared network capacity a single service can use, and improving alerting so we can find the source of connection surges faster.
Actions, Pages and Webhooks are operating normally.

We’re seeing recovery following mitigation and are continuing to monitor.

incidents.title: Incident with Actions, Pull Requests and Issues

updates.body:
On October 12th 2026 11:51 UTC GitHub experienced elevated 500 responses across several application pages. This caused failures on Issues and Pull Requests as well as Projects and Actions. Customers also experienced delayed notifications in their web inbox and via email.

The immediate impact to Issues, Pull Requests, Projects, and Actions was mitigated by 12:41 UTC on October 12th. Notifications deliveries to the web inbox and via email were recovering at 15:27 UTC and fully mitigated by 20:16 UTC.

The incident was triggered through a latent condition in our notifications delivery pipeline that put a high volume of an expensive query on our sharded database replicas. This reduced available database capacity to serve requests for Issues, Pull Requests, Projects, and Actions.

We have fixed the notifications pipeline’s code path that issued the expensive query. We are also improving resilience of the database layer to reduce the likelihood and impact of similar incidents.

incidents.title: Incident with Git Operations, Pull Requests and Actions

updates.body:
On October 7, 2026, GitHub had two outages of write operations with the same cause, totaling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC (about 10 minutes) and the second from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC (about 9 minutes). In both windows, actions that save or change data failed across Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. Reading data was largely unaffected.

In the first outage, 5.6% of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9%, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26% of Git authentication requests failed, and 17% of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second outage, 6.2% of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3%, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25% of Git authentication requests failed, and 19% of Actions workflow runs failed. No databases experienced data loss, and operations retried after recovery succeeded.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records, which still listed database servers we had already retired. When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers.

Each outage ended when one of our established machines with correct configuration became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. After the first outage, we identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. At 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honor the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again. We shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and have since removed it, and the automation now honors the pause, which was a new regression due to an update of our puppet infrastructure.

To prevent recurrence, we are clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, and we are keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked. We are also changing our systems to reject configuration that point to servers that don't exist and to keep using the last known-good settings instead. Finally, we are giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

We will share a more detailed write-up of these incidents in our monthly availability report, along with the status of the repairs we are making to prevent issues like these in the future.

incidents.title: Several services are degraded

updates.body:
On October 6, 2026, from 19:44 to 19:50 UTC, GitHub experienced a service outage with elevated error rates peaking at 1.30% of all requests, totaling approximately 1.16 million failed requests. This impacted 12 services across GitHub, including Pull Requests, Webhooks, Repos, OAuth, Git over SSH, Codespaces, and Gists. The incident was triggered by GitHub Enterprise Importer (GEI) making multiple, long duration queries which saturated a database connection pool. Recovery was seen at approximately 19:50 UTC once the migration's calls stopped; GEI migrations were reenabled at 23:32 UTC after a code fix was merged.

We have completed a detailed root-cause review and are implementing improved database-health safeguards. We will continue to review and add additional safeguards to prevent future recurrence.
